Comment "CLAUDE" and I'll send you all 3 repos.

Most people install Claude Code and then never touch a plugin. That's the whole gap. Three free ones, 189,000 GitHub stars between them, and each fixes something you've probably just been putting up with.

Here's what each one does:

1. Claude Setup shows you what your setup is missing. It's Anthropic's own plugin, 35,800 stars. Point it at your codebase and it names the skills and MCPs worth adding. Most people are running a fraction of what they could be.

2. OmniRoute means you never hit a usage limit. It routes you through 352 providers and 150+ of them cost nothing. MIT licensed, 60,500 stars. Hit a wall on one model and it swaps you to another so you keep working.

3. claude-mem makes Claude remember your whole project. 93,000 stars. It saves every session and hands it back the next time you open Claude. No re-explaining what your app does at the start of every chat.

All three install in about a minute. One line per plugin, straight into your terminal, no config and no accounts.

Free, open source, and built by people who use Claude Code every day.

Comment "PROMPT" and I'll send you the 7 prompts I actually reuse.

You don't need a smarter model. You need a clearer ask. Most bad output is a brief problem, not a model problem.

Here are the 7 habits:

1. Keep a prompt bank before you need one. Thinking one up on the spot never works. Under pressure you type "make it better" and get exactly that back.

2. Start with the work you already do. Don't start with what AI can do. Look at the last five hours of your own week and pick the thing that took longest.

3. Add the details that let it picture the job. Say who reads it and how long it should be. Two real details beat any prompt template.

4. Give it a goal and a hard limit. An ask with no rules gets you a wall of text. Say what winning looks like and where to stop.

5. Don't hide the part that went wrong. Most people open a fresh chat when it breaks. That bad answer is your best next prompt.

6. Make the prompt bigger than one chat. A prompt you typed once dies in that window. A prompt you saved runs on every job after it.

7. Cut it until only the useful part is left. Read it back. If you'd skim it, so will the model.

Stop waiting for a smarter model. Start writing a clearer ask.

Comment "CODE" and I'll send you the 7 files I start every project with.

Claude Code isn't hard. Asking for things properly is. Most people quit in week one because they type "it's broken" and get back a guess.

Here are the 7 steps:

1. Save the command before you need it. Retyping your setup every session is why people give up. Write it down once and it becomes one word.

2. Point it at work you already have. Don't start by building something new. Open the folder you already work in and ask it something about that.

3. Give it something it can look at. "It's broken" makes it guess. Paste the actual error and name the file. It only knows what you handed it.

4. Tell it where to stop. With no limit it wanders into files you never mentioned. Name the one file it's allowed to touch, approve the plan, then let it type.

5. Paste the error, don't start over. Most people open a fresh session the moment something breaks. That break is the most useful thing you own.

6. Turn the good prompt into a file. A prompt you typed once dies with the session. A Claude Skill gets pulled in whenever a job needs it.

7. Cut the session back to nothing. A long session isn't a smart one. Every old message rides along on every new answer, so type /clear between jobs.

Stop waiting to feel technical. Start pointing it at real work.

Comment "TOKENS" and I'll send you the full video walkthrough.

You're not hitting the limit because you use Claude too much. You're hitting it because you pay for the same chat over and over.

Nothing drops out of a conversation on its own. Every old message rides along again on every single turn.

Here's how to stop the bleeding:

1. Audit before you cut. Type /context and look at it. Every block in there is a token you already bought. My last session was 95% waste and 5% the actual job.

2. Kill the connectors you forgot about. Every connected app loads its whole tool list into every session, used or not. Disconnect the ones you never open.

3. Clear it, don't compact it. Compacting re-reads the entire thread and charges you for it again. Clearing costs nothing. Type /clear between jobs.

4. One session, one model. Switching models mid chat replays your history into the new one.

5. Batch your questions into one message instead of five.

6. Edit the message you got wrong instead of adding a correction underneath it.

7. Stop sending Opus to fetch things. Type /model and drop a tier. Opus for the hard calls, Sonnet for daily builds, Haiku for lookups.

None of this costs anything. It's all just what gets resent.

Comment "GENIUS" and I'll send you the full video walkthrough.

Everyone can spot an AI built page now. It stopped looking bad a while ago. It never stopped being obvious.

There are five tells, and six prompts that fix them.

Here's what's actually going wrong:

1. Slop has a look. Same typeface on every page, indigo into violet, three feature cards, one rounded corner on everything, frosted glass over a fake headline. Ask Claude to check your page against those five and name the ones you broke.

2. Claude doesn't know what good design is. So show it one. Give it any page you love and tell it to match the type, spacing and palette.

3. Ask for honest gaps, not praise. It'll tell you it looks great. Make it prove that instead. Ask for the three biggest gaps between your page and the one you love.

4. You can't fix what isn't measured. "Cleaner" is an opinion. A type scale is a number. Ask for the exact values, line height and corner radius included.

5. Screenshot it, then rebuild it. Any design you love is about three steps from being yours.

6. Save the rules once. New chats forget everything. A pasted file doesn't.

Stop prompting it and start directing it.

Comment "HARNESS" and I'll send you the full video walkthrough.

China just shipped a free version of Claude Code. 141,000 GitHub stars in 96 hours, MIT licensed, and it runs on your own machine.

It's called DeepSeek Harness. If you're new to this, here's the part that makes it click:

The model is the brain. The harness is the body. Claude Code is a harness. So is this one, and this one is free.

What you actually get:

1. One app, every model. Pick the brain from a dropdown. Frontier model when the work is client facing. Cheap model when you're running volume. Local model when the data must stay private.

2. The app is $0. The words aren't. Harness plus DeepSeek V4 Flash costs $0.03 per million words in and $0.10 out. Claude Code plus Opus 5 costs $5.00 in and $25.00 out. Same app price, very different bill at the end of the month.

3. Every part of it can be swapped. All 159 plugins ship switched on. Turn off the ones you don't want, rewrite the ones you do.

So which one do you actually open? Harness runs any model you like, it's MIT with the source included, and you get a web UI, a CLI or Python. It's also still a developer preview, so expect it to wobble. Claude Code is Claude models only and closed source, but it's production ready across your terminal, IDE, Slack and CI.

Run the free one for bulk work. Keep the paid one for client work.

Comment "MCP" and I'll send you the setup for all 5.

Claude on its own can only talk. MCPs are what give it hands. Wire these in once and it stops asking you to paste things in.

Here's the stack:

1. Playwright gives Claude your browser. It clicks, fills out forms and grabs data off any page, even ones with no API. Free and open source, one install line.

2. Firecrawl hands Claude the open web. It turns any page into clean text Claude can actually read and use. Free tier is 500 credits and there's no card required.

3. Perplexity turns Claude into a real researcher. Every answer comes back with a live source instead of a guess. The MCP is free, but it needs a paid Perplexity API key to run.

4. Higgsfield gives Claude a video team. It generates and edits your video and images, then upscales them, without leaving the chat. Free to connect, you pay credits per generation.

5. Blotato hands Claude your social accounts. Connect it once and Claude writes, schedules and posts to 9 platforms for you. This one's $29 a month with a 7 day trial, so it isn't free.

Two of these cost nothing at all. Start with those two and add the rest when a job actually needs them.

One word before your prompt changes the whole answer you get back.

Type /human before any rewrite and you get plain English back, not corporate speak.

Type /critic before you ship anything and it stops being polite, it lists the real risks.

Type /teacher when you're new to a topic and it explains it in plain words, one step at a time.

Type /brief when you want the three actions that matter, not the long warm up.

Type /compare when you're stuck choosing a tool and you get a table, not an opinion.

Five words. Nothing to install. Way better answers.

Comment "GOOGLE" and I'll send you all six with a guide for each.

6 Google AI tools you can start using today for free.

Gemini writes, plans, researches and makes images. Give it a real task, not a test question.

Gemini Notebook (used to be NotebookLM) only answers from the files you upload. Every line points back to your source.

AI Studio lets you test models and prompts free before you build anything.

Stitch turns one sentence into real app screens, so you design before you write a line of code.

Opal chains prompts and tools into one small app you can share with a link.

Antigravity hands an agent your editor, terminal and browser and it runs the whole task. Free for individuals while it's in preview.

You don't need a budget to start building with AI, you need these six tabs.
